opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because a lot of what teams are doing right now is compensating for the models' current limitations, and some of that work is going to get washed away with the next generation. If you spent months building elaborate prompt chains to get around a reasoning gap, there's a decent chance that gap closes and the scaffolding just isn't needed anymore.

But there are a few things I'm pretty confident stay valuable no matter how good the models get.

The first is evaluation. Knowing what "good" looks like for your application, having test sets that reflect your real users and your real risks, and being able to measure whether a change made things better or worse. That doesn't go away when the model gets smarter. If anything it matters more, because more capable systems get deployed in higher-stakes settings, and you need to know whether they're actually doing what you think they're doing. Teams that invest in a solid measurement practice can swap models, upgrade, and iterate quickly. Teams that don't are basically flying blind every time something changes.

The second is understanding your use case and your users deeply. What problem are you actually solving, what does failure look like, who gets harmed if it goes wrong? Models don't answer that for you. That product and domain thinking, plus the policy decisions about what the system should and shouldn't do, is human work that carries forward.

Third, the system-level safeguards and the architecture around the model: how you handle data, permissions, grounding in trusted sources, monitoring in production, human oversight in the places that matter. This is especially true as we move toward agents taking actions in the world. A smarter model doesn't remove the need for good identity controls or for limiting what it can touch. Defense in depth is a durable investment.

And finally, the operational muscle: the processes for red teaming, incident response, getting feedback from production back into your evals. That organizational capability compounds over time.

So my advice is usually: be a little careful about over-investing in clever workarounds for today's model weaknesses, and invest heavily in measurement, understanding your domain, and the guardrails and processes around the system. Those are the things that make you faster and safer with every new model, rather than things you have to throw away.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation, representative test sets, and measuring real user risks remain valuable as models improve.

r002.rationale: It mentions grounding in trusted sources, but does not clearly state that supplying relevant contextual data through retrieval or data augmentation will remain part of future applications.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify improvements to pipelines that deliver appropriate data to models as a durable investment.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot, because so much of what we do today can feel like scaffolding around the limitations of the current models. Some of it will absolutely go away. But I'd push back on the idea that most of it is temporary.

The piece I'm most confident will remain valuable is the work of actually understanding what you want the system to do. Writing down what "good" looks like for your application, building evaluation sets, figuring out how to measure whether the system is behaving the way you intend. That's not a workaround for model weakness. That's just engineering. As models get more capable, if anything, that work gets more important, because the space of things the model can do gets bigger, and so the question of what it should do in your particular context gets harder, not easier.

The second thing is the responsible AI and safety layer. People sometimes assume that as the models improve, all of the mitigation work becomes unnecessary. I don't think that's right. A more capable model is a more capable model, in every direction. You still need to understand your users, understand the risks in your specific scenario, have monitoring, have the ability to intervene. The specific techniques will change. Where I used to spend a lot of time on prompt engineering tricks to reduce a particular failure mode, that might get solved in the base model. But the discipline of thinking about failure modes, red-teaming your application, and designing for the case where something goes wrong will stay.

The third thing is grounding and integration. Connecting the model to your data, your tools, your systems of record, in a way that's secure and governed. That's not going to disappear with a better model, because the model doesn't know your business. It never will, unless you connect it.

What I expect to be less durable is a lot of the very hand-tuned orchestration. The elaborate chains, the brittle parsing, the many special-case prompts. Those feel to me like the things that get absorbed as the models get better at planning and following instructions.

So my advice to teams is usually to invest where the value accrues regardless of which model you're using. Know your problem deeply, know how to measure it, and build the infrastructure to adopt a better model quickly when it arrives.

r001.rationale: The response says risk analysis, red-teaming, monitoring, and planning for failures will remain valuable as models improve.

r002.rationale: It predicts that grounding models by connecting them to relevant data will continue to matter, even as models improve.

r003.rationale: It says secure, governed integration connecting models to data and systems will not disappear, communicating that investment in delivering relevant data to models remains valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think the work that starts with understanding what people actually need will remain valuable. What problem are you trying to solve? What does a good outcome look like? And how do you evaluate whether the system is delivering that outcome? A more capable model doesn’t answer those questions for you.

Some of the things we do today to work around model limitations will become unnecessary. So I’d be careful about investing too heavily in a particular workaround. But building evaluations, understanding the risks in your application, and creating a feedback loop with users—those investments help you take advantage of better models, too. They give you a way to tell whether a new model actually makes your product better.

r001.rationale: The response says that understanding application risks and building evaluations will remain useful with better models, which communicates continued risk-focused testing.

r002.rationale: It does not mention retrieval, data augmentation, or supplying models with relevant contextual data.

r003.rationale: It discusses avoiding investment in specific workarounds, but does not identify improving data-delivery pipelines as a lasting investment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the work to understand what you actually want the system to do—and how you’ll know whether it’s doing that well—is going to remain valuable. Better models don’t remove the need for good evaluations. You still need to understand your users, the context they’re operating in, and what kinds of mistakes matter for your application.

Some of the techniques we use to work around a particular model’s limitations will change. You might not need the same elaborate prompt with the next generation. But if you’ve built a good evaluation set, you can see whether that new model actually improves your system and where you still need safeguards.

And then there’s the application itself: connecting the model to the right information and tools, designing the interaction, and figuring out where a person needs to be involved. As models improve, you can revisit those choices, but the investment in understanding the problem carries forward.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations will remain valuable and emphasizes identifying which mistakes matter and where safeguards are needed, communicating continued value in checking models for application risks.

r002.rationale: It says applications involve connecting models to the right information, and that those choices can be revisited as models improve. This conveys the continued role of supplying relevant information to models.

r003.rationale: The response mentions connecting models to the right information, but does not identify improving data-delivery pipelines as an investment whose value will persist.
